people.name: Billy Murray
people.summary: The most-recorded American voice of the acoustic era and the definitive interpreter of Tin Pan Alley's comic and patriotic songs, heard on Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol cylinders from 1908 into the 1920s.
people.biography:
William Thomas Murray was born in Philadelphia on 25 May 1877 to Irish immigrant parents and raised in Denver, Colorado, which gave him the billing he never quite escaped — "the Denver Nightingale." He left home for the minstrel and vaudeville stage in his teens, and by the turn of the century was working the West Coast circuits. His first records were made in San Francisco around 1897 for the Peter Bacigalupi concern; by 1903 he had come east and was cutting cylinders for Edison's National Phonograph Company and discs for Victor and Columbia.

Murray's voice was not beautiful in any conventional sense, and that was the point. It was bright, hard-edged, nasal in the upper middle, and above all *audible* — a voice engineered, whether by accident or design, for the acoustic recording horn. Every consonant landed. Where a trained concert tenor produced a wash of tone that the diaphragm could not resolve, Murray produced words. That, more than anything, explains why he became the busiest recording artist in America for roughly two decades and why his records still sound startlingly present.

He was the voice of the era's comic songs — "Yankee Doodle Boy," "Grand Old Rag," "Under the Anheuser Bush," "Come, Josephine, in My Flying Machine," "Casey Jones," "K-K-K-Katy," "Oh Johnny, Oh Johnny, Oh!" — and of George M. Cohan's whole flag-waving catalogue. He led the American Quartet on Victor and the same singers as the Premier Quartet on Edison, sang duets with Ada Jones that are among the most beloved records of the period, and partnered Will Oakland, Elsie Baker and later Aileen Stanley. On four-minute cylinders he is inescapable: Edison Amberols from 1908, Blue Amberols from 1912 onward (many of the later ones dubbed from Diamond Disc masters), and issues on Indestructible and U-S Everlasting besides.

The microphone was less kind to him than the horn had been. Electrical recording arrived in 1925 and the bright, forced projection that had made him indispensable now sounded dated. He worked on into the 1930s with Victor and on radio, largely in supporting roles, and retired to Freeport, Long Island. He died there of a heart attack on 17 August 1954. Collectors of four-minute cylinders will own more Murray than anything else, and there is no better single artist through which to hear what the popular song of 1908–1920 actually sounded like.

people.name: Ada Jones
people.summary: The first woman to become a genuine recording star, and the era's great dialect comedienne — Bowery girls, Irish maids, coy sweethearts and squabbling wives, mostly in duet with Billy Murray or Len Spencer.
people.biography:
Ada Jane Jones was born in Oldham, Lancashire, on 1 June 1873, and came to Philadelphia with her family at the age of six. She was on the stage as a child, made a handful of brown-wax cylinders for Edison in 1893 while still in her teens, then dropped out of recording for a decade — a common enough pattern before the industry could pay a living wage. She returned around 1904, and within two years was the most important female voice in the American catalogue.

What she offered was range of *character*, not range of pitch. Jones could be a Bowery tough girl, an Irish immigrant, a German dialect wife, a Southern belle, a small child, or a coquettish young woman half her age, and the recording horn caught all of it. Her diction was as sharp as Murray's, and she had a comedienne's timing that survives the surface noise intact. Solo she recorded "I've Got Rings on My Fingers," "Row, Row, Row" and dozens of coon songs and rags; in duet she was one half of the two most successful partnerships of the period, with the monologist Len Spencer in vaudeville sketches such as the "Heinie" and "Flanagan" series, and with Billy Murray in flirtation numbers — "Shine On, Harvest Moon," "Come, Josephine, in My Flying Machine," "Be My Little Baby Bumble Bee."

She recorded for essentially everyone: Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol, Victor, Columbia, Indestructible, U-S Everlasting and the smaller labels. By the late 1910s her health was failing and the fashion for dialect comedy was fading. She kept working the small-time vaudeville circuits and died on tour in Rocky Mount, North Carolina, on 2 May 1922, aged 48. Her records remain the best surviving evidence of what American vaudeville actually sounded like from the stalls.

people.name: W. Van Brunt
people.summary: Edison's principal young ballad tenor of the Amberol and early Blue Amberol years, who reinvented himself in the 1920s under the name Walter Scanlan.
people.biography:
Walter Van Brunt was born in Brooklyn on 22 April 1892 and was recording professionally before he was eighteen. Edison signed him in 1910, and for the next several years he was the company's house tenor for sentimental ballads and light popular songs — the voice you hear on an enormous proportion of Edison Amberol and early Blue Amberol issues, often billed simply as "W. Van Brunt." He recorded solo, in duet with Ada Jones and Elizabeth Spencer, and as a member of Edison's quartets.

His was a clean, sweet, unforced lyric tenor with excellent diction and no operatic pretension, ideally suited to the four-minute cylinder's demand for a singer who could sustain a long verse-and-chorus ballad without straining. He also recorded for Victor, Columbia, U-S Everlasting and the dime labels, frequently under his own name.

In the early 1920s he began appearing as **Walter Scanlan** — a name adopted for the Irish-tenor stage repertoire associated with William J. Scanlan, and one he used on record labels and in vaudeville thereafter. Collectors regularly encounter the same voice under both names, and the two identities belong to one man. He lived until 11 April 1971. Because his Edison work spans exactly the four-minute cylinder's commercial life, a Van Brunt record is one of the most reliable ways to hear the Amberol format at its ordinary working best.
people.notes: The Van Brunt / Scanlan identity is well documented. Cylinder labels most often read 'W. Van Brunt' or 'Walter Van Brunt'; the Scanlan name belongs mainly to his later disc and stage career.

people.name: Byron G. Harlan
people.summary: Tenor and rural-dialect comedian, remembered both for lachrymose 'mother and child' ballads and for his twenty-year comic partnership with Arthur Collins.
people.biography:
Byron George Harlan was born in Paris, Kansas, on 29 August 1861 and came to recording by way of the minstrel stage and small-town theatre work in the Midwest. He began making cylinders in the late 1890s and by the mid-1900s was one of the busiest men in the New York studios.

He had two distinct careers on record. As a straight tenor he specialised in the sentimental tear-jerker — songs about dying children, absent mothers and old homesteads, of which "Always in the Way" and "School Days" are typical — sung with a plain, slightly grainy sincerity that Victorian audiences found irresistible and modern listeners find either touching or unbearable. As a comedian he worked in rube and New England rustic dialect, sometimes under character names such as Cyrus Pippins and Deacon Treadway.

His lasting fame is the duo. From about 1903 to 1926 Collins and Harlan were the most successful comic vocal team in America: Collins the rolling ragtime baritone, Harlan the higher, drier foil. They recorded hundreds of sides — "Alexander's Ragtime Band," "Under the Anheuser Bush," "Down in Jungle Town," "The Preacher and the Bear" — for Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol, Victor, Columbia, Indestructible, U-S Everlasting and every dime label going. Much of their repertoire is coon song and racial caricature, and is uncomfortable listening today; it is also, unavoidably, a large part of what four-minute cylinders were used for. Harlan's recording career wound down in the mid-1920s and he died on 11 September 1936.
people.notes: Several further pseudonyms are attributed to Harlan in the collector literature (Bert Terry, Byron Holland, Chester Lincoln among them). They are plausible but not uniformly documented, so only the best-attested character names are listed in aliases.

people.name: Arthur Collins
aliases: The King of the Ragtime Singers
people.summary: Billed in his day as 'the King of the Ragtime Singers', Collins was the leading baritone of the coon-song and ragtime repertoire and half of the famous Collins and Harlan team.
people.biography:
Arthur Francis Collins was born in Philadelphia on 7 February 1864 and worked in light opera and minstrel companies before the phonograph found him in the mid-1890s. He had a big, dark, rhythmically springy baritone with the kind of forward attack the acoustic horn loved, and an unfailing sense of syncopated timing. Between about 1898 and the early 1920s he was among the two or three most recorded male voices in the United States.

His repertoire was dominated by ragtime songs and coon songs — "The Preacher and the Bear," "Bill Bailey, Won't You Please Come Home," "Hello! Ma Baby," "Alexander's Ragtime Band" — sung in the exaggerated black dialect that white recording artists of the period used as a matter of routine. The results made him a star and make him difficult listening now; the historical record is what it is, and Collins's rhythmic authority is genuinely remarkable regardless of the material.

From 1903 he was paired with the tenor Byron G. Harlan, and Collins and Harlan became the defining comic duo of the acoustic era. Collins recorded for every company that mattered — Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol, Victor, Columbia, Zon-o-phone, Indestructible, U-S Everlasting — and appeared on four-minute cylinders in enormous quantity. An accident on stage in 1921, when he fell through an open trapdoor, effectively ended his performing career. He retired to Tice, Florida, and died there on 2 August 1933.

people.name: Collins and Harlan
aliases: Arthur Collins and Byron G. Harlan
people.summary: The most successful comic vocal duo of the acoustic era: baritone Arthur Collins and tenor Byron G. Harlan, recording together from about 1903 to 1926.
people.biography:
Collins and Harlan were not a group in the sense of an ensemble with a fixed membership — they were two established solo artists whose voices happened to fit together so well that record companies billed them as a unit for more than twenty years. Arthur Collins supplied the heavy, syncopated baritone lead; Byron G. Harlan the lighter, drier tenor above it, and the comic straight-man timing.

Their catalogue runs to several hundred titles and covers the whole territory of American popular comedy between 1903 and the mid-1920s: ragtime and coon songs, rube dialect sketches, novelty numbers, and topical songs about automobiles, aeroplanes, telephones and Prohibition. "Alexander's Ragtime Band" (1911) was their biggest hit and remains one of the best-selling records of the acoustic period. On four-minute cylinders they appear on Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol, on Indestructible and on U-S Everlasting, frequently with the credit line "Comic duet with orchestra."

Much of the material trades in racial caricature and is genuinely offensive; it also documents, more completely than any other source, what a mass audience was laughing at in the years before the First World War. The partnership wound down after Collins's stage accident in 1921 and ended entirely by 1926.

people.name: Vernon Dalhart
people.summary: Light-opera tenor turned the first commercially successful country recording artist, and the acoustic era's champion user of pseudonyms — at least eighty verified names on record labels.
people.biography:
Marion Try Slaughter was born on 6 April 1883 in Jefferson, Texas, and built his stage name from two Texas towns, Vernon and Dalhart, between which he had punched cattle as a boy. He trained seriously as a singer at the Dallas Conservatory, moved to New York in 1910, and worked in light opera — he sang in *H.M.S. Pinafore* and in Puccini's *Girl of the Golden West* — before Edison auditioned him in 1916. Thomas Edison himself is said to have approved the voice, and Dalhart became a mainstay of the Edison catalogue, appearing on Blue Amberol cylinders and Diamond Discs in ballads, light classics and, increasingly, southern dialect songs.

In 1924 he recorded "The Wreck of the Old 97" backed with "The Prisoner's Song" for Victor. It became one of the best-selling records of the entire 78 era, sold in the millions, and effectively invented the commercial country record. Dalhart spent the rest of the decade making event songs, disaster ballads and sentimental rural numbers for every label that would have him.

And that is the root of his pseudonym problem. Because the same performance was licensed and re-recorded across labels selling at wildly different prices, companies issued him under invented names to keep a seventy-five-cent Victor and a twenty-five-cent dime-store disc from carrying the same artist. At least eighty pseudonyms have been verified — Al Craver on Columbia, Tobe Little on OKeh, Vel Veteran on Grey Gull, and dozens more, many applied without his knowledge. A cylinder or disc credited to a name no reference book recognises is, more often than for any other artist of the period, Vernon Dalhart.

The Depression and the rise of authentic rural performers ended his career. He died in Bridgeport, Connecticut, on 14 September 1948, working as a night clerk and voice teacher, and was elected to the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1981.
people.notes: Only the best-attested pseudonyms are listed. The full list runs past eighty names, many of them label-invented and disputed between discographers.

people.name: Manuel Romain
people.summary: Minstrel-show tenor whose high, plaintive ballad style made him one of Edison's most characteristic Amberol voices in the years around 1910.
people.biography:
Manuel Romain came out of the New England minstrel tradition, working for years with Dockstader's and other blackface companies before the phonograph made him nationally known. He recorded chiefly for Edison from around 1907, and his voice — an unusually high, soft, almost keening tenor, more head-voice than chest — is one of the most recognisable on Amberol cylinders.

His repertoire was sentimental almost without exception: mother songs, Irish ballads, songs of parting and of dead sweethearts, delivered with an unhurried rubato that four minutes of playing time suited perfectly. "Meet Me To-night in Dreamland," "Silver Bell" and similar titles show the manner. He also recorded for Indestructible and U-S Everlasting, and remained a vaudeville draw into the 1920s.

Romain died on 22 December 1926. To modern ears his style can seem impossibly lachrymose; to Edison's customers in 1910 he was the sound of a good ballad well sung, and he sold in large numbers.

people.name: Will Oakland
people.summary: A countertenor of extraordinary range whose falsetto-tinged high voice was a novelty and a sensation on Edison cylinders from 1908; later a New York nightclub proprietor.
people.biography:
Born Herman Hinrichs on 15 January 1880, Will Oakland possessed the rarest voice in commercial American recording: a genuine high countertenor, capable of a sustained soprano-like line that most listeners assumed must be a woman. He began recording for Edison in 1908, at exactly the moment the four-minute Amberol was introduced, and his records were among the format's early curiosities and successes.

He recorded Irish ballads, sacred songs and sentimental numbers as a soloist; sang with the Peerless Quartet and led his own Will Oakland Quartet; and made duets with Billy Murray in which he took the woman's part in love songs — a conceit audiences found delightful rather than odd. He worked for Edison, Victor, Columbia, Indestructible and U-S Everlasting, and "Silver Threads Among the Gold" was among his signature titles.

As recording fashions changed Oakland moved into management, running the Chateau Shanley and later his own Terrace Garden in New York. He died on 15 May 1956. A four-minute cylinder with his name on the label is instantly identifiable within two bars.

people.name: Irving Kaufman
people.summary: One of the most prolific singers ever to record in the United States, and — after Dalhart — the era's most heavily pseudonymed artist.
people.biography:
Irving Kaufman was born Isidore Kaufman in Syracuse, New York, on 8 February 1890, the son of Russian Jewish immigrants. He began recording in 1914 and simply never stopped: estimates of his output run to many thousands of issued sides across Victor, Columbia, Edison, Vocalion, Gennett, Emerson, Harmony and the entire tribe of dime-store labels. He worked with his brothers Jack and Phil as the Kaufman Brothers in vaudeville and on record.

His voice was a bright, flexible, slightly reedy tenor with a natural feel for the syncopated popular song, and he made the transition from acoustic to electrical recording more comfortably than most of his contemporaries. On four-minute cylinders he appears on late Blue Amberols, generally dubbed from Edison Diamond Disc masters, and on Indestructible.

The cheap labels that bought his services issued him under an extraordinary number of invented names — Jim Andrews, Tom Frawley, Frank Harris, Robert Wood, Marvin Young, Noel Taylor and many more — so that a collector who cannot identify a mid-1920s tenor on an obscure label should always consider Kaufman first. He continued singing on radio into the 1930s and 1940s and lived until 3 January 1976.
people.notes: Kaufman's pseudonym list is long and partly conjectural; only names repeatedly attested in the discographical literature are given here.

people.name: Elizabeth Spencer
people.summary: Edison's most-recorded female singer, a dramatic soprano who made several hundred sessions for the company between about 1910 and 1916.
people.biography:
Elizabeth Dickerson Spencer was born on 12 April 1871 and became, in sheer volume, the most heavily recorded woman in the Edison catalogue. Her sessions for Edison Standard, Amberol and Blue Amberol between roughly 1910 and 1916 number in the hundreds — a figure no other Edison vocalist of either sex approached in the same period.

She had a warm, full dramatic soprano and an unusually adaptable one. She sang sacred songs and hymns, sentimental parlour ballads, light operatic excerpts and popular duets, and she was the standard female partner for Edison's house tenors — Walter Van Brunt above all, but also Harry Anthony and later Charles Hart. Her voice was steady enough for the acoustic horn and expressive enough to carry a four-minute ballad without monotony, which is precisely what an Amberol needed.

Because she worked almost entirely for one company, she is far better known to cylinder collectors than to disc collectors. She died on 22 April 1930.

people.name: Anna Case
people.summary: Metropolitan Opera lyric soprano and Edison's favourite Tone Test artist, whose recordings anchor the Royal Purple Amberol series.
people.biography:
Anna Case was born in Clinton, New Jersey, on 29 October 1887, the daughter of a blacksmith, and had no conservatory training of the usual sort — she paid for lessons out of her own earnings and made her Metropolitan Opera debut in 1909 without ever having sung in Europe first. She remained at the Met until 1916, then built a long and lucrative career in concert and on the vaudeville stage.

Edison prized her above almost any other singer. Her voice was pure, bright and evenly produced, with the kind of steadiness the acoustic process rewarded, and she became the central figure in his famous Tone Tests — public demonstrations in which a live singer performed alongside her own recording and the audience was invited to detect the difference when the lights went down. She recorded extensively for Edison on Diamond Disc and on Blue Amberol, and her operatic and art-song titles were among the mainstays of the purple-dyed Royal Purple Amberol series issued from 1918.

Case later married the industrialist Clarence Mackay and largely withdrew from professional singing, though she remained an active patron of music. She died on 7 January 1984, aged 96, having outlived the entire cylinder industry by more than half a century.

people.name: Miss Marie Narelle
aliases: The Australian Queen of Irish Song
people.summary: Australian soprano billed as 'the Australian Queen of Irish Song', whose 1906 Edison sessions Edison himself praised as the best-recorded soprano voice he had heard.
people.biography:
Born Catherine Mary Ryan on 28 January 1870 in New South Wales, Marie Narelle took her stage name from Mount Narelle near her childhood home. She won the soprano championship at the Sydney Eisteddfod, went to the United States for the 1904 St Louis World's Fair as the official Australian singer, and stayed to build an international concert career on Irish and Australian song.

She recorded for Edison in 1906, and the company reported that her voice took to the recording horn better than any soprano they had yet tried — a claim repeated in Edison advertising for years afterwards. Her Edison titles, mostly Irish ballads and sacred songs such as "Killarney" and "Sweet Spirit, Hear My Prayer," were originally issued as two-minute Gold Moulded records and several were carried forward onto four-minute Amberol and Blue Amberol issues as the catalogue was rebuilt for the longer format.

She toured Britain and Ireland extensively, settled in England, and died on 26 January 1941. For Australian collectors she is a landmark figure: one of the first Australian-born singers to achieve genuine international recording fame.

people.name: Henry Burr
people.summary: The great ballad tenor of the acoustic era, a Peerless Quartet mainstay and one of the most recorded singers of the century's first three decades, issued under a dozen different names.
people.biography:
Harry Haley McClaskey was born on 15 January in St Stephen, New Brunswick, and came to New York as a young man to study voice, intending an operatic career. The recording studios intervened. From about 1902 he made records under a bewildering assortment of names — Irving Gillette for Edison, Alfred Alexander, Robert Rice, Carl Ely, Harry Barr, Al King and others for various companies — before settling on Henry Burr as his principal identity.

Burr's voice was a smooth, high, plangent lyric tenor with a controlled vibrato and impeccable enunciation, and he applied it almost exclusively to the sentimental ballad. It made him one of the best-selling artists of the era: "Let Me Call You Sweetheart," "I'm Sorry I Made You Cry," "Just a Baby's Prayer at Twilight," and dozens more. He sang duets with Albert Campbell for well over a decade, was a member and later the manager of the Peerless Quartet, and sang in the Sterling Trio and the Columbia Stellar Quartette.

On four-minute cylinders he appears on Edison Amberol (usually as Irving Gillette, because of his contracts elsewhere), on Indestructible, on Columbia Indestructible and on U-S Everlasting — his name and its aliases are a reliable index of how tangled acoustic-era exclusivity arrangements could get. In the 1920s and 1930s he moved into radio, becoming a fixture of the *National Barn Dance*. He died in Chicago on 6 April 1941.
people.notes: Sources conflict on his birth year: DAHR and several standard references give 1882, while Library and Archives Canada and the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame give 1885. Birth year is therefore omitted rather than guessed.

people.name: Albert Campbell
people.summary: First tenor of the Peerless Quartet and Henry Burr's long-standing duet partner, with a recording career running from the late 1890s to the 1920s.
people.biography:
Albert Charles Campbell was born in New York on 17 August 1872 and began recording in the late 1890s, when the industry was still selling cylinders one at a time from a recording horn. He had a light, sweet, high tenor that blended better than it soloed, and he built a career on exactly that quality.

He was a founding member of the Peerless Quartet and sang first tenor with it for most of its existence, was one third of the Sterling Trio with Burr and John H. Meyer, and spent well over a decade as Henry Burr's duet partner — the Burr and Campbell records of 1911 to 1925, including "The Trail of the Lonesome Pine," "Till We Meet Again" and "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles," were among the steadiest sellers of the period. He also sang with the American Quartet and various ad hoc studio groups.

Campbell appears on four-minute cylinders both as a soloist and, far more often, inside one ensemble or another; on Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol, Indestructible, and U-S Everlasting. He died on 25 January 1947.

people.name: Frank Croxton
people.summary: Bass soloist and quartet singer — Peerless Quartet, Stellar Quartette, the Croxton Quartet — and a voice teacher of standing.
people.biography:
Frank Croxton was born on 7 October 1877 and made his career as the sort of reliable, well-schooled bass every recording studio needed: solid at the bottom, accurate, and able to blend. He sang in the Peerless Quartet, the Columbia Stellar Quartette, the Trinity Choir and his own Croxton Quartet, and appeared as a bass soloist in sacred and concert repertoire on Edison, Victor and Columbia.

On four-minute cylinders he turns up chiefly in ensemble credits, and in sacred selections where a solid bass line was essential — hymn settings, gospel songs and the quartet arrangements that made up a large slice of both the Edison and the Indestructible catalogues. He taught singing for many years and died on 4 September 1949.

people.name: Len Spencer
people.summary: Pioneer recording baritone, monologist and vaudeville sketch artist, and Ada Jones's great comic partner in the 'Heinie' and 'Flanagan' dialogues.
people.biography:
Leonard Garfield Spencer was born in Washington, D.C., on 12 February 1867, the son of Platt Rogers Spencer's family of penmanship fame, and was among the very first Americans to make a living from recorded sound. He was recording brown wax in the early 1890s and by the turn of the century was one of the most reproduced voices in the country.

Spencer's speciality was the descriptive specialty — a recorded playlet with sound effects, dialogue and song, of which the most famous is "Arkansaw Traveler." He worked in dialect of every kind, ran a theatrical booking agency, and formed durable partnerships: the Len Spencer Trio with Steve Porter and Billy Golden, the Greater New York Quartette, and above all his series of vaudeville sketches with Ada Jones, in which the pair play courting couples, quarrelling immigrants and comic types of every nationality then available to the American stage.

By the four-minute era his own recording activity was tailing off, but his earlier material was extensively remade for Amberol and later dubbed to Blue Amberol, and the longer format suited his sketches better than the two-minute cylinder ever had. He died suddenly on 15 December 1914.

people.name: Harry Macdonough
people.summary: One of the defining tenors of the acoustic era, lead of the Haydn Quartet and later a Victor recording executive; 'Harry Macdonough' was itself a pseudonym.
people.biography:
John Scantlebury Macdonald was born in Hamilton, Ontario, on 30 May 1871, of Irish and Scottish descent. He began recording in the late 1890s and adopted the name Harry Macdonough — a stage pseudonym that stuck so firmly most listeners never knew his real one.

His tenor was smooth, cool and precise, the antithesis of Billy Murray's brash attack: an ideal ballad voice and an ideal quartet lead. He sang lead in the Haydn Quartet (originally the Edison Quartet) through its most successful years, in the Lyric Quartet and the Orpheus Quartet, and made a long series of duets with the contralto Alice Nielsen, with Elise Stevenson and with S. H. Dudley. Solo he recorded "In the Shade of the Old Apple Tree," "Blue Bell" and a great quantity of sacred and sentimental material.

His cylinder work belongs mostly to the two-minute era and the early Amberol years; much of it was carried onto four-minute issues in remade or dubbed form. He became a recording director for Victor in 1920 and left performing entirely. He died on 26 September 1931.

people.name: John Bieling
people.summary: First tenor of the Edison Quartet, the Haydn Quartet and the American Quartet — the top line of the most successful close-harmony groups of the period.
people.biography:
John Bieling was born in New York on 12 September 1869 and spent his career as the first tenor whose bright, penetrating top line sat above almost every important American male quartet of the acoustic era. He was in the Edison Quartet from its formation in 1896, which became the Haydn Quartet when the same four men recorded for other companies, and he was first tenor of the American Quartet from 1909 — the group that also recorded for Edison as the Premier Quartet.

He recorded occasional solos and duets, but his importance is as an ensemble singer: the American Quartet's records of "Casey Jones," "Moonlight Bay" and "Oh! You Beautiful Doll" are unimaginable without him. Vocal trouble forced him to retire from singing in 1913, after which he worked in the record business in other capacities. He died on 1 June 1948.

people.name: William F. Hooley
people.summary: The bass of the Edison, Haydn and American Quartets, and one of the most frequently recorded low voices of the acoustic era.
people.biography:
William F. Hooley was born in Ireland in 1861 and brought to the United States as a child. From 1896 he was the bass of the Edison Quartet — the Haydn Quartet under its other name — and from 1909 the bass of the American Quartet, which meant that for the best part of two decades his was the foundation under most of the best-selling close-harmony records made in America.

He recorded solos in sacred and patriotic repertoire and was a fixture of the Edison Mixed Quartet and the Trinity Choir, but it is the ensemble work that matters: a quartet record of this period rises or falls on the bass, and Hooley's was firm, warm and unfailingly in tune. He died on 12 October 1918, one of the many victims of the influenza epidemic.

people.name: Steve Porter
people.summary: Baritone of the American Quartet and Premier Quartet, and a prolific Irish-dialect comedian best known for his 'Flanagan' sketches.
people.biography:
Steve Porter was born in 1862 and recorded from the 1890s until the 1920s in two quite different capacities. As a baritone he sang in the American Quartet — and therefore, on Edison, in the Premier Quartet — as well as in the Peerless Quartet, the Empire Vaudeville Company and countless studio ensembles.

As a comedian he wrote and performed the long-running "Flanagan" series of Irish-dialect sketches, in which a stage Irishman blunders through the modern world: Flanagan at the barber's, on the farm, at the vocal teacher's, and so on. Several were recorded with Ada Jones and other studio regulars, and the four-minute cylinder gave the format enough room to develop a joke properly, so Amberol and Blue Amberol versions are common. Porter also recorded straight ballads and sacred numbers. He died on 13 May 1936.

people.name: S. H. Dudley
people.summary: Baritone of the Edison and Haydn Quartets under a stage name, and later the author of Victor's celebrated 'Victrola Book of the Opera'.
people.biography:
Samuel Holland Rous recorded under the name S. H. Dudley from the 1890s, singing baritone in the Edison Quartet from its formation in 1896 and thereafter in the Haydn Quartet, as well as making solo records and duets with Harry Macdonough. The pseudonym was adopted early and used consistently; it should not be confused with the African-American vaudeville manager Sherman H. Dudley, an entirely different man.

Rous left performing to work on the editorial and catalogue side of the Victor Talking Machine Company, where he compiled *The Victrola Book of the Opera*, a guide that ran through many editions and shaped how a generation of American record buyers understood opera. He was born in 1864 and died in 1947. His cylinder work belongs mainly to the two-minute era, but his quartet recordings were remade and dubbed for four-minute issue.
people.notes: Not to be confused with Sherman H. Dudley (1872–1940), the Black vaudeville performer and theatre-circuit owner who also billed himself S. H. Dudley.

people.name: Frank C. Stanley
people.summary: Bass singer and pioneering recorded banjoist, a Peerless Quartet founder whose career was cut short at the very start of the four-minute era.
people.biography:
William Stanley Grinsted, who recorded as Frank C. Stanley, was born on 29 December 1868 and was one of the first banjoists ever committed to a commercial record. He soon proved more valuable as a bass singer, and by the 1900s was among the busiest men in the studios: a founding member and manager of the Peerless Quartet, a member of the Columbia Male Quartette, and the bass half of a great many duets and trios — with Henry Burr, with Elise Stevenson, with Corinne Morgan, and with Byron G. Harlan.

He was also a competent baritone soloist in sacred and sentimental repertoire. Stanley died on 12 December 1910, aged 41, just as the Amberol cylinder was establishing itself, so his four-minute output is comparatively small and his records appear on early Amberols, Indestructible and U-S Everlasting issues rather than on the Blue Amberols that came later.

people.name: Harry Anthony
people.summary: Sacred-music tenor who recorded as 'Harry Anthony' until 1912 and thereafter under his real name, John Young; half of the era's leading hymn duo with James F. Harrison.
people.biography:
John Young used the pseudonym Harry Anthony from the beginning of his recording career until about 1912, when he began appearing under his own name; Edison and other companies continued to print the pseudonym on some labels even after his catalogues acknowledged the real one. He was one of the principal tenors of the acoustic era's enormous sacred-music trade.

From 1905 he was paired with the baritone Frederick J. Wheeler, who recorded as James F. Harrison, and the duo Anthony and Harrison became the standard American recording of the hymn repertoire: "The Holy City," "Lead, Kindly Light," "Abide With Me," "Nearer, My God, to Thee." Their records sold steadily for well over a decade and appear on Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol, Indestructible, Columbia and Victor. Young also sang in the American Quartet, the Peerless Quartet and the Trinity Choir.

The sacred four-minute cylinder was a substantial commercial category in its own right — sold to churches, to Sunday schools and to households that would not buy a ragtime record — and Anthony and Harrison were its central figures.
people.notes: Some reference works give the pseudonym as a company invention rather than the singer's own choice; the point is disputed.

people.name: James F. Harrison
people.summary: The baritone half of the sacred duo Anthony and Harrison; his real name was Frederick J. Wheeler, and he recorded under both.
people.biography:
Frederick J. Wheeler recorded under the pseudonym James F. Harrison, and from 1905 formed with the tenor John Young — billed as Harry Anthony — the most successful sacred vocal duo of the acoustic period. Their first joint recording was an Edison cylinder, and the partnership ran for well over a decade across Edison Amberol and Blue Amberol, Victor, Columbia and Indestructible.

Wheeler also recorded as a soloist under his own name, sang in quartets, and worked as a chorus director. Collectors will find the same voice credited both ways, sometimes on records issued within months of one another by different companies — a small but characteristic illustration of how the industry used names to manage exclusivity.

people.name: Reinald Werrenrath
people.summary: Concert and Metropolitan Opera baritone who recorded popular ballads under the pseudonym Edward Hamilton to protect his classical billing.
people.biography:
Reinald Werrenrath was born in Brooklyn on 7 August 1883, the son of a Danish tenor, and became one of the leading American concert baritones of his generation. He sang at the Metropolitan Opera, gave recitals across the country, and was among the earliest serious singers to take radio seriously.

His relevance to cylinder collectors is twofold. He recorded art song, opera and patriotic material under his own name for Victor and Edison — repertoire of exactly the sort the Royal Purple Amberol series existed to carry. And, because a concert artist could not be seen to sing "When You and I Were Young, Maggie" for the general catalogue, he recorded a large quantity of popular ballad and quartet material under the pseudonym **Edward Hamilton**. The two names belong to one voice, and the Hamilton records are the ones a four-minute cylinder collector is most likely to meet.

Werrenrath later conducted and taught. He died on 12 September 1953.

people.name: Charles W. Harrison
people.summary: Prolific ballad tenor of the 1910s, heard on almost every label of the period including Edison's four-minute cylinders.
people.biography:
Charles W. Harrison was one of the standard ballad tenors of the 1910s — a clear, well-produced lyric voice of the type the industry could not have too many of, since the sentimental song was the single largest category in every catalogue. He recorded for Victor, Columbia, Edison, Emerson and a long list of smaller labels, sang in studio quartets, and made numerous duets.

His best-known titles include "They Didn't Believe Me" and a great many wartime and post-war ballads. He should not be confused with James F. Harrison, the pseudonym of Frederick J. Wheeler, nor with the several other Harrisons active in the studios at the same time — a confusion the record companies did nothing to discourage.

people.name: Charles Hart
people.summary: Tenor of the Shannon Four and a busy Edison and Columbia soloist in the years around the First World War.
people.biography:
Charles Hart was one of the workhorse tenors of the late acoustic period. He recorded prolifically as a soloist and in duet with Elliott Shaw and with Lewis James, and was an original member of the Shannon Four — the quartet formed in 1917 that later became the Shannon Quartet and, by 1926, the Revelers.

His Edison work appears on Diamond Discs and, dubbed from them, on late Blue Amberol cylinders, which is how most collectors of four-minute cylinders encounter him. The voice is a bright, straightforward lyric tenor without idiosyncrasy — a professional studio singer of the sort the industry ran on.

people.name: Lewis James
people.summary: Tenor who joined the Shannon Four in 1918 and went on to sing with the Revelers; a fixture of late-acoustic ensemble and solo recording.
people.biography:
Lewis James replaced Harvey Hindermyer in the Shannon Four in 1918 and stayed with the group through its transformation into the Shannon Quartet and then the Revelers, the smooth close-harmony act that carried the quartet tradition into the electrical era and influenced the Comedian Harmonists and much else besides.

As a soloist and duettist he recorded extensively for Victor, Edison and Columbia, mostly in ballads and light popular material. His Edison sides reached four-minute cylinder buyers as Blue Amberol dubbings of Diamond Disc masters.

people.name: Harvey Hindermyer
people.summary: Tenor, original member of the Shannon Four, later famous on radio as one of the Gold Dust Twins.
people.biography:
Harvey Hindermyer was an original member of the Shannon Four, singing with the group from its formation in 1917 until 1918, when Lewis James took his place. Before that he had built a solid recording career of his own; his biggest solo success was a 1908 Columbia recording of "Take Me Out to the Ball Game."

He recorded for Edison, Columbia and other labels in ballads and popular songs, and made duets with the contralto Helen Clark. In the 1920s he found a second career in broadcasting as one of the Gold Dust Twins, an early and hugely popular sponsored radio act.

people.name: Sam Ash
people.summary: Broadway and vaudeville tenor who recorded popular songs for Edison, Columbia and others in the 1910s.
people.biography:
Sam Ash was a musical-comedy tenor of the 1910s who divided his time between the Broadway stage and the recording studio. He recorded popular songs, wartime numbers and light ballads for Columbia, Edison and several smaller labels, and his Edison work reached cylinder buyers on Blue Amberol.

He is a good example of a category that matters for anyone reading four-minute cylinder labels: the working stage singer with a real but modest recording career, whose name appears on a handful of issues and then vanishes from the catalogues.

people.name: George Wilton Ballard
people.summary: Edison house tenor of the Blue Amberol years, heard in ballads, novelty songs and duets.
people.biography:
George Wilton Ballard was one of the tenors Edison relied on through the Blue Amberol period, recording ballads, comic and novelty songs and a good deal of duet material. He appears both on Diamond Discs and on Blue Amberol cylinders, many of the latter dubbed from the disc masters after 1915.

His voice is a light, agreeable lyric tenor with clean diction — again, exactly what the Edison recording department wanted for the four-minute format. He is one of those artists almost unknown outside cylinder collecting yet extremely common within it.

people.name: Helen Clark
people.summary: Edison contralto of the Blue Amberol era, prolific in duets with Harvey Hindermyer, Walter Van Brunt and Joseph Phillips.
people.biography:
Helen Clark was one of the principal female voices in the Edison catalogue during the Blue Amberol years, recording both as a contralto soloist and — more often — as the lower voice in duets. Her partnership with Harvey Hindermyer produced a long series of records, and she also sang with Walter Van Brunt, Joseph A. Phillips and others.

Her repertoire was the standard mixture of sentimental ballads, sacred songs and popular numbers of the day, including "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles." She recorded on both Edison cylinder and disc formats and appears throughout the Blue Amberol popular series.

people.name: Gladys Rice
people.summary: Edison soprano of the late 1910s and 1920s, best known for her duets with Vernon Dalhart and Billy Murray.
people.biography:
Gladys Rice sang for Edison through the later Blue Amberol years, recording light popular songs, operetta selections and a substantial run of duets — with Vernon Dalhart above all, but also with Billy Murray and other house artists. Her voice is a bright, agile light soprano well suited to the musical-comedy repertoire that dominated Edison's popular list after the war.

Her records reached the cylinder catalogue as Blue Amberol dubbings from Diamond Disc masters, which is true of nearly all Edison material issued after about 1915 and is worth remembering when judging the sound of a late cylinder.

people.name: Agnes Kimball
people.summary: American soprano popular on Victor, Columbia and Edison records in the 1910s, whose career ended with her early death in 1918.
people.biography:
Agnes Kimball was born in October 1881 and became a well-known recording soprano during the 1910s, working for the Victor Talking Machine Company, Columbia and Edison. She recorded ballads, sacred songs, operetta excerpts and duets, and her records were issued in both disc and four-minute cylinder form.

She died on 5 January 1918, at thirty-six. Her comparatively short career means her name appears on a compact and fairly identifiable body of records, which makes her a satisfying artist for collectors to pursue.

people.name: Christine Miller
people.summary: Concert contralto who sang in the very first of Edison's Tone Tests, and a mainstay of the company's sacred and art-song lists.
people.biography:
Christine Miller was a Pittsburgh-born concert contralto with a rich, even, unforced tone that recorded exceptionally well by the acoustic process. Edison used her heavily in the oratorio and sacred repertoire — "The Rosary," "Abide With Me," excerpts from *Messiah* and *Elijah* — and in art songs and ballads.

Her place in phonograph history is secured by the Tone Tests. In February 1915, at a demonstration in Orange, New Jersey, Miller sang alongside her own recording, the lights were lowered, and the audience was invited to say which was which. The stunt became the centrepiece of Edison's marketing for the next decade and Miller was its first subject. Her records appear on Diamond Disc and on Blue Amberol cylinder, including in the Royal Purple series.
people.notes: Birth and death years follow the dates commonly given in Edison and Tone Test literature; they are not attested by a single authoritative source.

people.name: Thomas Chalmers
people.summary: Metropolitan Opera baritone who recorded exclusively for Edison, and later a film actor and documentary editor.
people.biography:
Thomas Hardie Chalmers was born in New York on 20 October 1884, studied in Italy, and sang leading baritone roles at the Boston Opera and then at the Metropolitan Opera between 1917 and 1922. He made all his commercial recordings for Edison, which gives him an unusual concentration in the Edison catalogues.

His range on record is wide: operatic arias, art songs, Scottish and Irish folk songs, sacred numbers and sentimental ballads, issued on Diamond Disc and on Blue Amberol cylinder, with the more serious material appearing in the Royal Purple Amberol series. He was a favourite Tone Test artist as well.

Chalmers left singing for the theatre in the 1920s, acted on Broadway and in films, and worked as a narrator and editor of documentaries, notably Pare Lorentz's *The Plow That Broke the Plains*. He died on 12 June 1966.

people.name: Marie Rappold
people.summary: German-born Metropolitan Opera dramatic soprano and an Edison celebrity artist, central to the Tone Test campaign and the Royal Purple Amberols.
people.biography:
Born Marie Winterrath in London to German parents, Rappold was raised in New York and sang at the Metropolitan Opera from 1905 to 1920. Edison recruited her as one of his flagship celebrity artists, and she recorded opera arias, art songs and duets for the company on Diamond Disc and Blue Amberol.

According to Edison's own account, the first public comparison test between a live singer and a record took place at Carnegie Hall on 28 April 1916 with Rappold providing the live voice — the demonstration that grew into the nationwide Tone Test tours. Her records were among the prestige items in the Royal Purple Amberol series, the purple-dyed classical line Edison launched in 1918.

She died in North Hollywood on 12 May 1957.
people.notes: Sources disagree on her year of birth — 1872 and 1879 both appear in reputable references — so it is omitted here.

people.name: Arthur Middleton
people.summary: American bass-baritone of the Metropolitan Opera and a leading Edison concert artist of the Royal Purple period.
people.biography:
Arthur Middleton was born in Logan, Iowa, on 28 November 1880 and studied with Charles R. Adams and Alexander Emslie. He made his Metropolitan Opera debut in 1914 and sang secondary roles there through early 1916, but his real career was on the concert and oratorio platform, where a big, dark, firmly produced bass-baritone was worth more than it was in the opera house.

Edison recorded him extensively in oratorio, opera and patriotic material — the kind of repertoire the four-minute cylinder handled well, since arias and sacred solos rarely fit comfortably into two minutes. His records appear on Diamond Disc and on Blue Amberol, including in the Royal Purple series.

He died in Chicago on 16 February 1929, the same year the Blue Amberol itself was discontinued.

people.name: Alice Verlet
people.summary: Belgian coloratura soprano, active mainly in France, who became one of Edison's featured celebrity recording artists.
people.biography:
Alice Verlet was born in Belgium in 1873 and made her career principally in France as a lyric coloratura soprano. In the United States she was known chiefly as a concert singer, and she became a featured Edison artist — the company built a good deal of publicity around her flexible, brilliant top register, which the acoustic process captured better than it captured heavier voices.

Her Edison recordings of French and Italian coloratura repertoire were issued on Diamond Disc and on Blue Amberol cylinder, and she is one of the European names a collector will meet in the Royal Purple Amberol range. She died in Paris in 1934.

people.name: Guido Ciccolini
people.summary: Italian tenor and Edison celebrity artist, a familiar name in the Royal Purple Amberol series.
people.biography:
Guido Ciccolini was born in Rome in 1885 and settled in the United States, where he became one of Edison's contracted operatic tenors. He recorded Italian arias, Neapolitan songs and light classical material for the company, appearing on Diamond Disc and on Blue Amberol cylinder.

His records are among the most frequently encountered in the Royal Purple Amberol range — the purple-dyed classical series in the 29000 numbers issued from 1918 — including titles such as "Funiculi, Funicula" with chorus. He died in Neptune, New Jersey, in 1963.

links.label: Search the Cylinder Audio Archive for Guido Ciccolini

people.name: Carolina Lazzari
people.summary: Operatic contralto contracted to Edison in the late 1910s and heard in the Royal Purple Amberol series.
people.biography:
Carolina Lazzari was an American operatic contralto of Italian descent who sang with the Chicago Opera Association and in concert, and who recorded for Edison during the years when the company was assembling a roster of exclusive classical artists to compete with Victor's Red Seal.

Her arias and art songs were issued on Diamond Disc and carried onto Blue Amberol cylinder, including in the Royal Purple series. She is a good example of the second tier of Edison celebrity artists — well regarded in her day, thoroughly documented on record, and largely forgotten outside collecting circles.

people.name: Mary Jordan
people.summary: American concert contralto who recorded art song, sacred music and folk arrangements for Edison and Columbia.
people.biography:
Mary Jordan was a concert contralto of the 1910s who recorded for Columbia and for Edison, chiefly in art songs, hymns, and arrangements of Irish and Scottish folk material. Her voice was deep and steady in the way the acoustic horn liked, and she was used in the same repertoire slots as Christine Miller.

Her Edison sides reached cylinder buyers on Blue Amberol, and she is another of the concert singers whose presence in the four-minute catalogue reflects Edison's determination to sell more than popular songs.

people.name: Betsy Lane Shepherd
people.summary: Edison soprano of the Blue Amberol period, recorded in ballads, sacred songs and light classics.
people.biography:
Betsy Lane Shepherd was one of the sopranos Edison kept on hand through the Blue Amberol years for ballads, hymns and light classical selections. She recorded on Diamond Disc and on cylinder, and appears in duet as well as solo credits.

Like several Edison house singers, she is almost invisible in general reference works and thoroughly familiar to anyone who reads Edison supplements — a reminder of how much of the four-minute catalogue was carried by capable professionals who never became famous.

people.name: Elliott Shaw
people.summary: Baritone of the Shannon Four and later the Revelers, and a prolific duet and ensemble singer in the late acoustic era.
people.biography:
Elliott Shaw was the baritone of the Shannon Four from its formation in 1917, staying with the group as it became the Shannon Quartet and then the Revelers. He was also one of the busiest ensemble singers of the late acoustic and early electrical periods, recording for Victor, Edison, Columbia and Brunswick.

His duets with Charles Hart were widely issued, and his Edison work reached cylinder buyers on late Blue Amberols. His importance is representative rather than individual: the four-part male harmony sound of American records between about 1917 and 1930 is largely the sound of Shaw and his colleagues.

people.name: Wilfred Glenn
people.summary: Bass of the Shannon Four and the Revelers, and a much-recorded ensemble and solo singer.
people.biography:
Wilfred Glenn sang bass in the Shannon Four from 1917 and remained with the group through its Shannon Quartet and Revelers incarnations, becoming one of the most familiar low voices on American records. He also recorded solos in sacred and comic repertoire and sang with the Trinity Choir and numerous studio ensembles.

On four-minute cylinders he appears within ensemble credits on late Blue Amberols dubbed from Edison Diamond Disc masters.

people.name: Joseph A. Phillips
people.summary: Baritone active on Edison and other labels in the 1910s, frequently heard in duets with Helen Clark.
people.biography:
Joseph A. Phillips was a baritone of the 1910s who recorded ballads, sacred songs and popular numbers for Edison, Columbia and other companies. He is met most often in duet, particularly with the contralto Helen Clark, and in quartet work.

His Edison material appears on Blue Amberol cylinder as well as on disc, and he is one of the reliable second-rank names that fill out the middle of the four-minute catalogue.

people.name: John H. Meyer
people.summary: Bass of the Peerless Quartet and the Sterling Trio, active from the 1900s into the 1920s.
people.biography:
John H. Meyer sang bass in the Peerless Quartet for much of its long life and was the third voice of the Sterling Trio alongside Henry Burr and Albert Campbell. He also recorded with the American Quartet and in a variety of ad hoc studio groups.

A collector meeting his name on a four-minute cylinder label will nearly always be looking at an ensemble credit; solo Meyer records are comparatively scarce. He is nonetheless one of the voices most often present, unnoticed, on the quartet records that made up a large share of Amberol, Blue Amberol, Indestructible and U-S Everlasting output.

people.name: Donald Chalmers
people.summary: Bass who sang with the American Quartet and other studio ensembles in the 1910s.
people.biography:
Donald Chalmers was one of the basses who passed through the American Quartet after William F. Hooley's death in 1918, and who sang in a range of studio groups in the later 1910s. He recorded sacred and popular material and appears in ensemble credits on Victor and Edison issues, including four-minute cylinders.

He should not be confused with the Edison operatic baritone Thomas Chalmers, an unrelated artist recording for the same company at the same time.

people.name: Vaughn De Leath
people.summary: Pioneer radio singer credited with developing the soft 'crooning' style, and a recording artist for Edison and many other labels in the 1920s.
people.biography:
Vaughn De Leath was among the first singers to broadcast — by her own account she sang over Lee de Forest's experimental station in 1920 — and she built a career on being the voice of early radio. The story that she invented crooning is a simplification, but there is truth in it: she found that a soft, low, close-in delivery survived the primitive transmitters that a full-voiced soprano would overload, and audiences liked it.

She recorded prolifically through the 1920s for Edison, Columbia, Gennett, Okeh and others, in popular songs, novelty numbers and early jazz-inflected material. Her Edison sides were issued on Diamond Disc and dubbed to Blue Amberol, so she is one of the last significant new voices to appear on a four-minute cylinder before the format was discontinued in 1929. She died on 28 May 1943.

people.name: Aileen Stanley
people.summary: Vaudeville headliner and one of the biggest-selling women on record in the 1920s, in duets with Billy Murray among others.
people.biography:
Aileen Stanley was born in Chicago in 1893 and worked her way up through vaudeville to become one of the highest-paid and most-recorded women in American popular music during the 1920s. Her manner was intimate and conversational rather than declamatory, and it translated well from stage to record and then to radio.

She recorded chiefly for Victor, with sides for Edison, Gennett and others, and made a celebrated series of duets with Billy Murray in the mid-1920s — an odd and delightful pairing of the old acoustic shouter with a modern popular stylist. Her Edison material reached the four-minute cylinder catalogue on late Blue Amberols. She retired from performing in the 1930s, taught singing, and died in 1982.

people.name: Ernest Hare
people.summary: Baritone and comic singer, half of the Happiness Boys with Billy Jones and one of the most heavily pseudonymed artists of the 1920s.
people.biography:
Ernest Hare was a baritone with a broad comic delivery who recorded from the mid-1910s and became, in partnership with the tenor Billy Jones, one of radio's first stars. As the Happiness Boys — named for their sponsor, Happiness Candy Stores — Jones and Hare broadcast weekly from 1921 and made hundreds of records of novelty songs, topical comedy and popular numbers.

Hare recorded for practically every label of the 1920s, frequently under invented names, and appears on late Edison Blue Amberol cylinders through Diamond Disc dubbings. He died on 9 March 1939.

people.name: Billy Jones
people.summary: Tenor and comedian, the other half of the Happiness Boys, prolific on records and on early network radio.
people.biography:
Billy Jones was a light comic tenor who began recording around 1919 and quickly became one of the busiest men in the studios. With Ernest Hare he formed the Happiness Boys, whose weekly broadcasts from 1921 made them among the first genuinely national radio personalities in the United States.

Jones recorded solo and in duet for dozens of labels, often pseudonymously, in novelty songs, comic numbers and the popular hits of the day. Edison issued him on Diamond Disc and, by dubbing, on Blue Amberol cylinder in the format's final years. He died on 23 November 1940.

people.name: Al Bernard
people.summary: New Orleans-born blackface singer and one of the first white artists to record blues material, active on Edison and many other labels.
people.biography:
Al Bernard was born in New Orleans in 1888 and worked in minstrelsy and vaudeville before beginning to record around 1918. He was among the earliest white performers to record blues — his versions of W. C. Handy's "St. Louis Blues" and "Hesitating Blues" were commercially important, and Handy himself thought well of him — though he performed in blackface and in dialect throughout his career.

He recorded for Edison, Brunswick, Emerson, Okeh and many others, sometimes with the guitarist Frank Ferera, and his Edison sides were dubbed to Blue Amberol cylinder. He later worked in radio and songwriting. He died in 1949. His records sit at an awkward and revealing junction between minstrelsy and the beginnings of the commercial blues record.

people.name: Cal Stewart
people.summary: Creator of 'Uncle Josh Weathersby' of Punkin Center, the most durable comic character in the history of recorded sound.
people.biography:
Calvin Edward Stewart was born in Charlotte County, Virginia, in 1856 and worked as a railwayman, a medicine-show performer and a vaudevillian before finding the character that made him. Uncle Josh Weathersby is an elderly New England farmer from the fictional village of Punkin Center who visits the city, encounters modern life, and reports back — Uncle Josh at the dentist's, on an automobile, in a department store, joining the Grangers, at the roller-skating rink.

The records are essentially stand-up monologues punctuated by Stewart's celebrated wheezing laugh, and they sold continuously from the late 1890s until well after his death. Stewart recorded for Edison, Victor, Columbia and — importantly for cylinder collectors — for Indestructible, whose four-minute celluloid cylinders carried a large body of his work and are among the most sought-after comic records of the period. The Amberol's four minutes suited him far better than the two-minute cylinder had, since a monologue needs room to build.

He died on 7 December 1919. His characters were revived by imitators for years afterwards, and Punkin Center passed into American folklore largely because of him.

links.label: Search the Cylinder Audio Archive for Cal Stewart

people.name: Nat M. Wills
people.summary: Vaudeville's 'Happy Tramp', whose parody songs and topical monologues were a staple of the four-minute cylinder.
people.biography:
Nat M. Wills, born Louis McGrath Wills on 11 July 1873, built one of vaudeville's most recognisable acts around a tramp persona — battered hat, ruined dress suit, unhurried patter — and a specialty in parody. He would take the hit songs of the moment and fit them with new topical words about politics, marriage, Prohibition or the cost of living, and the results were among the sharpest comic records of the period.

He recorded for Victor, Columbia and Edison, and his monologues and parodies were well suited to the four-minute format, which allowed him to develop a routine rather than truncate it. "No News, or What Killed the Dog" is his most famous record, a slow-building shaggy-dog monologue that has never quite gone out of circulation.

Wills died on 9 December 1917 of carbon monoxide poisoning in his own garage, at forty-four.

people.name: Billy Golden
people.summary: Blackface minstrel comedian and one of the earliest recording artists, later half of the duo Golden and Hughes.
people.biography:
Billy Golden was among the first performers to make commercial records at all, cutting brown wax cylinders in the early 1890s. His speciality was blackface minstrel comedy and dialect song, and his hits — "Turkey in the Straw," "Rabbit Hash," "Roll On the Ground" — remained catalogue staples for thirty years, being remade repeatedly as recording technology changed.

In 1907 he formed a duo with Joe Hughes; Golden and Hughes were among the first two-man teams to record blackface dialogue, and their sketches were issued widely on four-minute cylinders, including by Indestructible and U-S Everlasting as well as Edison. They were a substantial vaudeville draw as well.

The material is minstrelsy through and through and reads badly today. Its commercial importance to the cylinder business, however, was very large, and Golden's long career maps the medium's first three decades almost exactly. He died in 1926.

people.name: Joe Hughes
people.summary: Blackface comedian and Billy Golden's partner from 1907 in the recording duo Golden and Hughes.
people.biography:
Joe Hughes joined Billy Golden in 1907 to form one of the first two-man blackface comedy teams to record extensively. Golden and Hughes made dialogue sketches, comic songs and laughing records for Edison, Victor, Columbia, Indestructible and U-S Everlasting, and worked the vaudeville circuits with the same material.

Hughes is documented almost entirely through the partnership; little of his life outside it is recorded. The team's four-minute cylinders are common enough that any collector of comic Amberols will meet them.

people.name: Bert Williams
people.summary: The greatest American comedian of his generation and the first Black performer to star on Broadway; his 'Nobody' is among the era's defining records.
people.biography:
Egbert Austin Williams was born in Nassau, the Bahamas, on 12 November 1874 and raised in California. With George Walker he formed Williams and Walker, the most successful Black act in American vaudeville, and their 1903 musical *In Dahomey* was the first full-length Broadway show written and performed by African Americans. After Walker's illness and death Williams became a solo star and, from 1910, the featured comedian of the Ziegfeld Follies — the first Black performer to headline a white Broadway production.

He worked in blackface, as the industry required even of Black performers, and made from that constraint a character of extraordinary melancholy and precision: a slow-moving, put-upon, unlucky man whose timing was legendary. W. C. Fields called him the funniest man he ever saw and the saddest man he ever knew.

Williams recorded for Victor and, from 1901, extensively for Columbia. His signature song "Nobody" (1905, remade 1913) is one of the essential American records of the era, and his talking songs — half-sung, half-spoken, with immaculate rhythmic placement — anticipate a great deal of later popular performance. Columbia issued his material widely, and titles reached four-minute cylinder buyers through the Columbia Indestructible series. He died on 4 March 1922 after collapsing on stage.

people.name: Eddie Morton
people.summary: Vaudeville comic singer known as 'The Singing Cop', a forceful and rhythmically striking recording artist of the ragtime era.
people.biography:
Edward Farren Morton was born in Philadelphia on 15 May 1870 and had been a policeman before he went on the stage, which gave him his billing. He became a headliner on the Keith and Poli circuits and one of the most distinctive singers of the ragtime era on record: a big, blunt, hard-swinging baritone with a rhythmic drive unusual even among his contemporaries.

He recorded for Victor, Columbia, Edison and Indestructible in comic and ragtime numbers — "Alexander's Ragtime Band," "Oh, You Kid" and the like — and his four-minute cylinders are among the liveliest comic records of the period. He died on 11 April 1938.

people.name: Bob Roberts
people.summary: Leading exponent of the comic coon song in the 1900s, heard on Zon-o-phone, Edison, Indestructible and the cheaper cylinder labels.
people.biography:
Bob Roberts was one of the most prolific comic singers of the 1900s, specialising in the ragtime and coon-song repertoire that dominated popular recording before the First World War. He recorded a great deal for Zon-o-phone and for the cheaper labels, as well as for Edison, Columbia and Indestructible.

Typical titles include "Wouldn't It Make You Hungry" and "I'm Satisfied." His delivery was raucous, rhythmic and unsubtle, and it sold; he was one of the artists on whom the early cylinder trade depended for comic material, and his records appear regularly among four-minute issues.

people.name: Edward M. Favor
people.summary: Light-comedy stage star and recording tenor, celebrated for Irish-American comic songs delivered in a piping high tenor.
people.biography:
Edward M. Favor was already a well-established musical-comedy performer when he began recording in the 1890s — a contemporary notice in 1900 called him one of the best light comedians on the American stage. He kept recording for the next decade and more, in comic songs, Irish-American numbers and stage material.

His voice was a light, piping, unmistakably theatrical tenor and his diction was excellent, which mattered a great deal when the joke was in the lyric. He recorded for Edison, Columbia, Victor and the cylinder labels, and his material carried onto four-minute issues. He died in 1936.

people.name: Edward Meeker
people.summary: Edison's staff announcer — the voice that names the title and the company at the head of countless cylinders — and a comic singer in his own right.
people.biography:
Edward Meeker was born on 22 January 1874 and worked for Edison in West Orange for most of his career. To cylinder collectors he is first of all a *voice*: the studio announcer who opens innumerable Edison records with the formula naming the title, the composer and "Edison Record." Spoken announcements were dropped from most issues after 1908, so hearing Meeker is one of the reliable signs of an early cylinder.

He was also a performer. He recorded comic and novelty songs — "Chicken Reel," "Go Easy, Mabel," "Harrigan" — and made the 1908 Edison recording of "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" that was added to the National Recording Registry in 2010. He died on 19 April 1937.

people.name: Arthur Fields
people.summary: Baritone and songwriter, ubiquitous on records from 1914, best known for wartime and novelty numbers.
people.biography:
Arthur Fields was born Abraham Finkelstein on 6 August 1888 and started in minstrel shows before moving into recording in 1914. From then until the early 1930s he was one of the most heavily recorded male voices in America, working for every significant label and a great many insignificant ones, often under assumed names.

His speciality was the topical and novelty song — First World War numbers above all, of which "Oh! How I Hate to Get Up in the Morning" is the type — sung in a bright, brassy, thoroughly extrovert baritone. He was also a working songwriter, with "Aba Daba Honeymoon" among his credits. His Edison recordings reached the cylinder catalogue as Blue Amberol dubbings. He died on 29 March 1953.

people.name: Harry Lauder
people.summary: The Scottish music-hall star who became the first British recording artist to sell a million records, and a fixture of the four-minute cylinder catalogues.
people.biography:
Sir Harry Lauder was born in Portobello, near Edinburgh, on 4 August 1870, worked as a pit boy in the coal mines, and rose through Scottish music hall to become the highest-paid entertainer in the world. The act — kilt, twisted walking stick, tam o'shanter, a stream of patter and a repertoire of his own songs — was a broad Scots caricature performed with immense charm and impeccable timing.

His songs are still known: "I Love a Lassie," "Roamin' in the Gloamin'," "A Wee Deoch-an-Doris," "Keep Right On to the End of the Road," the last written after his only son was killed on the Somme in 1916. He toured America more than twenty times and recorded for Gramophone, Victor and Edison; his material was issued on four-minute cylinders in both Britain and the United States, and Edison Blue Amberols of Lauder titles are common.

He was knighted in 1919 for his wartime entertainment and fundraising work and died on 26 February 1950. He is the single most important non-American artist in the four-minute cylinder catalogue.

people.name: Homer Rodeheaver
people.summary: Billy Sunday's song leader and the man who put the gospel song on commercial records in quantity.
people.biography:
Homer Alvan Rodeheaver was born on 4 October 1880 and became the music director for the evangelist Billy Sunday, leading vast revival choirs with a trombone and an unshakeable good humour. He was also a shrewd businessman who founded his own publishing house and understood earlier than most preachers that the phonograph could carry the gospel song into homes no revival tent would reach.

He recorded prolifically for Victor, Columbia and Edison from the 1910s, in solos, duets and with quartets, and his records made "Brighten the Corner Where You Are," "The Old Rugged Cross" and similar hymns into permanent fixtures of American religious life. Sacred material was a very large commercial category on four-minute cylinders, and Rodeheaver is its most significant single figure. He died on 18 December 1955.
